name: 55-Inch TV
blurb: A modern 55-inch LED TV draws 60–120 watts depending on brightness and content. Five hours of nightly viewing costs only a few dollars a month — brightness settings and always-on standby features matter more than screen time.
tips: Turn off 'store demo' or 'vivid' mode — it can nearly double panel power.
Enable the ambient light sensor so brightness drops in a dark room.
Disable quick-start/instant-on standby if you don't need voice wake; it can idle at 10–20 watts.

name: 65-Inch TV
blurb: Stepping up to 65 inches adds roughly 30–40% more panel area and a proportional bump in power, typically 80–150 watts in normal use. HDR content pushes brightness — and wattage — toward the top of that range.

name: 75-Inch TV
blurb: Large-format 75-inch and up TVs draw 100–250 watts, with bright HDR scenes hitting harder. Even so, a movie night costs less than the popcorn — big TVs are cheap to run relative to their presence.

name: OLED TV
blurb: OLED power scales with what's on screen: dark movies sip electricity while bright sports and HDR push draw well above a comparable LED set. On mixed content, expect a modest premium over an LED panel of the same size.

name: Home Theater Projector
blurb: Lamp-based projectors draw 250–400 watts, while modern laser and LED models often run half that. A couple of movie nights a week costs well under a dollar a month in most states.

name: Soundbar
blurb: Soundbars draw 15–60 watts at normal listening volume and under a watt in modern standby. As a bill item they round to zero next to the TV they sit beneath.

name: AV Receiver
blurb: AV receivers draw 80–400 watts depending on volume and channels driven, and older units can idle high in standby. If your receiver stays warm when 'off,' it's still drawing — a power strip fixes that.

name: Game Console (PS5 / Xbox Series X)
blurb: Current-generation consoles draw 150–220 watts in demanding games but only 30–70 watts streaming video. Rest mode with fast wake can add a constant trickle — the difference between standby modes is real money over a year.
tips: Use energy-saver standby instead of instant-on; overnight fast-wake costs add up all year.
Streaming apps on the console burn far more power than a streaming stick doing the same job.
Enable auto-off timers for controllers and the console itself.

name: Nintendo Switch (Docked)
blurb: The Switch is the efficiency champion of consoles, drawing 10–25 watts docked — about a tenth of a PS5. Even heavy daily play costs under a dollar a month everywhere in the U.S.

name: Cable / Satellite Box
blurb: Cable and satellite boxes are infamous standby offenders: many draw nearly the same 15–30 watts whether you're watching or not, 24 hours a day. Over a year, an always-on DVR box can consume more electricity than a new refrigerator.

name: Streaming Stick (Roku, Fire TV, Apple TV)
blurb: Streaming sticks and pucks draw 3–8 watts — the cheapest way to put apps on a TV. Replacing an old cable box with one eliminates a meaningful always-on load.

name: Smart Speaker
blurb: Smart speakers idle at 2–4 watts while listening for their wake word. Even a houseful of them costs only a dollar or two a month combined — convenience with a genuinely small footprint.

name: Record Player / Turntable
blurb: Turntables draw 5–30 watts including the phono stage — vinyl's running cost is effectively zero. The amplifier and speakers behind it are where the watts actually go.
